Stated Claim / Post Context:
Restoring nature at an unprecedented scale, solar overtakes nuclear as power source, interfaith mosque rebuilding

In today's edition: the world is making big progress in restoring damaged ecosystems, solar energy is quickly becoming a more substantial global power source than nuclear, and interfaith cooperation is rebuilding mosques shared by different religious communities in Punjab.

Actual Article Body:
Elizabeth Jacyshyn-Owen | Posted on November 2, 2026 |

Photo: Wesley Fernandes/Unsplash (CC0)

In today’s edition: the world is making big progress in restoring damaged ecosystems, solar energy is quickly becoming a more substantial global power source than nuclear, and interfaith cooperation is rebuilding mosques shared by different religious communities in Punjab.

A new UN report has revealed that approximately 252 million hectares of degraded land are now being restored worldwide, an area 5.6 times the size of Sweden. Wildlife is also making a comeback, with jaguars, snow leopards and dolphins among the species benefiting.

Source: Sweden Herald

Governments at the UN’s COP17 biodiversity conference in Armenia have agreed to speed up global nature protection efforts. The Yerevan Pathway sets priorities for 2030, including cutting harmful subsidies and increasing funding for developing countries. However, securing the necessary financial resources remains a major challenge.

Source: Reuters

A restoration project at Brazil’s Guapiaçu Ecological Reserve has planted 1 million native Atlantic Forest seedlings, and the efforts have also helped bring back lowland tapirs, with around 25 now living in the area after disappearing from Rio de Janeiro state in 1914.

Source: Ecoticias

Daily smoking in Spain has dropped to its lowest recorded level, with just 15.4% of people aged 15 and older smoking, down from 32.1% in 1993. However, smoking remains more common among men (18.4%) than women (12.6%), with significant differences linked to socioeconomic status.

Source: Democrata

According to new data, solar energy is growing faster than expected and is beginning to surpass nuclear power across the globe. Seven key factors explain its rise, from dramatically falling costs to expanding adoption.

Source: BBC News

After two decades of planning and construction, the SunZia project is now delivering wind power from New Mexico to California through a 550-mile transmission line, supplying more than 1 million homes and generating more electricity than the Hoover Dam.

Source: Grist

Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality, claims Eric Laakmann, the co-founder of Vessev, whose company builds fully electric hydrofoil boats. These vessels use underwater “wings” to lift their hulls above the surface as they pick up speed, reducing drag, one of the biggest obstacles to making boats more energy-efficient.

Source: The Guardian

Oyster farming in New Hampshire’s Great Bay is growing, with local farmers using floating equipment to boost production. One farm, Little Bay Beauties, now sells around 500,000 oysters annually – five times its previous output – and is seeking approval to expand by another 4.5 acres.

Source: NHPR

The American Exchange Project gives students from places like Utah, Texas and the Bronx the chance to experience unfamiliar communities across the United States. By immersing young people in different local cultures and ways of life, the programme aims to build empathy and connections across communities.

Source: Reasons To Be Cheerful

Villagers of various faiths in Punjab, India, are coming together to restore historical mosques that were abandoned or destroyed during the 1947 partition. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.

Source: The Guardian
